questions.question: Johannes Kepler's best model of Mars, built on a circle, fit almost every one of Tycho Brahe's sightings of the planet. Yet it missed some of them by eight arcminutes, about a quarter of the full Moon's width. Kepler threw the model out rather than let so small a gap pass. Why would he not accept the gap?
questions.answer: Tycho's own errors were far smaller than the gap
choices: Tycho's own errors were far smaller than the gap
Ptolemy's old circles had missed by less than that
Copernicus's circles had fit those sightings exactly
Galileo's telescope had shown the same gap
questions.context: Tycho, the last great astronomer to work without a telescope, fixed the planets' places to within about one or two arcminutes, so a miss of eight had to be the model's fault, not his; Kepler wrote that 'these eight minutes alone will lead us along a path to the reform of the whole of Astronomy.' Tables built on Ptolemy's circles had erred by more than 30 arcminutes, and Copernicus, who also used circles, died in 1543, long before Tycho's sightings. Galileo first turned a telescope on the sky late in 1609, the year Kepler's Astronomia Nova came out.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches that a result is judged against the uncertainty of the measurement, and Kepler's eight arcminutes is the classic case of a small, real mismatch overturning a model.

questions.question: Johannes Kepler spent years on Tycho Brahe's sightings of Mars, hunting for the true shape of the planet's path round the Sun. The shape he settled on, which he set out in his book Astronomia Nova in 1609, turned out to fit every planet. What did Kepler find?
questions.answer: An ellipse, with the Sun off its centre
choices: An ellipse, with the Sun off its centre
An ellipse, with the Sun at its centre
A circle, with the Sun off its centre
An egg shape, with the Sun near its broad end
questions.context: Kepler's first law: each planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, one of two points that lie off the centre along the ellipse's long axis. Kepler tried an off-centre circle and an egg shape first, and each missed Tycho's sightings by about eight arcminutes, the two in opposite directions. The planets' ellipses are nearly round, so even Mars's path, drawn to scale, would look almost like a circle with the Sun a little off centre.
questions.grade_note: Kepler's first law is the high-school statement of how planets orbit (NGSS HS-ESS1-4), and the Sun's place at a focus rather than the centre is the part students most often get wrong.

questions.question: In the Northern Hemisphere, winter runs from the December solstice to the March equinox and lasts about 89 days. Summer, from the June solstice to the September equinox, lasts about 94. Earth passes nearest the Sun in early January. Why is the northern winter the shorter season?
questions.answer: Earth moves faster along its path when nearer the Sun
choices: Earth moves faster along its path when nearer the Sun
The Sun's stronger pull in January holds Earth back
Earth's tilt shortens the season tipped away from the Sun
Earth spins faster on its axis in the winter months
questions.context: By Kepler's second law the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves fastest when nearest the Sun: Earth, about 147 million kilometres away in early January, crosses its winter stretch of orbit a few days quicker than its summer stretch, when it is about 152 million kilometres away. The tilt makes the seasons but not this difference, since in the south, where winter falls between June and September, winter is the longest season. The Sun's stronger pull in January speeds Earth up as it swings in, rather than holding it back.
questions.grade_note: Kepler's second law (fastest when nearest the Sun) is high-school content, and the uneven seasons are its everyday evidence, there on any calendar.

questions.question: Saturn lies about ten times as far from the Sun as Earth does. Yet one trip round the Sun takes Saturn about 29 of Earth's years, not 10. Why does Saturn take so long?
questions.answer: It moves along its path more slowly than Earth
choices: It moves along its path more slowly than Earth
Its path is stretched into a much longer oval
Its path climbs far above and below Earth's
It winds along its path in small loops
questions.context: Kepler's third law says the farther a planet lies from the Sun, the longer it takes to go round, and the year grows faster than the distance because the planet also moves more slowly: Saturn travels about 9.7 kilometres a second, a third of Earth's 29.8, on a path nearly as round as Earth's and tilted only 2.5 degrees from it. Newton explained why: ten times as far away, the Sun's pull is a hundredth as strong, and so weak a pull keeps a planet on its curved path only at a slower speed. Ptolemy and Copernicus built small circles called epicycles into the planets' paths, but Kepler's ellipses did away with them.
questions.grade_note: Kepler's third law in words (farther out, longer year) is in the high-school standards, and seeing that an outer planet also moves more slowly is the step beyond 'its path is longer'.

questions.question: Isaac Newton compared the Moon with a falling apple. The Moon lies about 60 times as far from Earth's centre as the apple does. In each second it curves toward Earth, away from a straight path, by only about 1/3,600 of the distance the apple drops in its first second. What does that show about Earth's pull?
questions.answer: It weakens with the square of the distance
choices: It weakens with the square of the distance
It weakens in step with the distance
It weakens with the cube of the distance
It weakens with the square root of the distance
questions.context: Sixty times sixty is 3,600, so a pull that weakens with the square of the distance is 1/3,600 as strong at the Moon as at the ground, just what the Moon's fall of about 1.4 millimetres a second shows beside the apple's 4.9 metres. So twice as far from any mass its pull is a quarter as strong, and the pull that drops an apple is the same one that holds the Moon on its path. A pull weakening in step with the distance would leave a sixtieth of its strength at the Moon, sixty times too much.
questions.grade_note: The inverse-square law of gravitation is in the high-school standards (NGSS HS-PS2-4), and Newton's Moon test is the standard evidence for it.

questions.question: Jupiter holds more than 300 times as much mass as Earth. In his Principia, Isaac Newton used his law of gravity to work out Jupiter's mass as a share of the Sun's, long before any spacecraft could fly past it. What did he use to weigh Jupiter?
questions.answer: How fast its moons circle it, at their distances
choices: How fast its moons circle it, at their distances
How fast it circles the Sun, at its distance
How wide it looks, at its distance from Earth
How bright it shines, at its distance from the Sun
questions.context: The stronger a planet's pull, the faster a moon at a given distance must go round to stay in orbit, so the four large moons Galileo found in 1610 gave Newton a Jupiter of about a thousandth of the Sun's mass, close to today's figure. A planet's own trip round the Sun says nothing of its mass: the Jupiter trojans, asteroids tiny beside Jupiter, share its path and take the same 12 years. Size and brightness show only how big and how bright a planet looks, not how much matter it holds.
questions.grade_note: High-school courses use Newton's law to predict the orbits of moons (NGSS HS-ESS1-4), and weighing a planet by its moons shows what the law can measure.

questions.question: Halley's comet took over a year longer to come round between 1531 and 1607 than between 1607 and 1682. Before its next return, Alexis Clairaut and two fellow mathematicians in Paris worked out that it would be held back by about 618 days, and it swung past the Sun on 13 March 1759, about a month from their date. What had they reckoned would hold it back?
questions.answer: The pull of Jupiter and Saturn as it passed them
choices: The pull of Jupiter and Saturn as it passed them
The drag of the thin gas lying between the planets
The push of sunlight on its long, glowing tail
The loss of the ice it boils off near the Sun
questions.context: Newton's law says every mass pulls on every other, so the comet feels Jupiter and Saturn as well as the Sun: Halley had blamed its uneven laps on those two planets, and Clairaut's team worked out that their pull would delay it by 618 days. Its arrival close to their date was one of the first great tests of Newton's law. Sunlight pushes a comet's tail away from the Sun, and the jets of gas from its ice shift its timing by only about four days.
questions.grade_note: High-school standards ask students to predict orbits from Newton's law (NGSS HS-ESS1-4), and the comet's late return in 1759 is a classic successful prediction that needed the planets' pull as well as the Sun's.

questions.question: Uranus kept drifting off the path that Newton's law of gravity gave it, running ahead of its predicted place for years and then falling behind. Urbain Le Verrier, in Paris, worked out what was causing the drift. On 23 September 1846 Johann Galle turned a telescope in Berlin to the spot Le Verrier gave him, and found that he was right. What had Le Verrier worked out?
questions.answer: An unseen planet farther out was pulling on it
choices: An unseen planet farther out was pulling on it
An unseen planet nearer the Sun was pulling on it
An unseen moon of its own was tugging at it
A passing comet had knocked it off course
questions.context: From the drift alone Le Verrier worked out where an unseen planet beyond Uranus had to be, as John Couch Adams did separately in England, and that night Galle and his assistant Heinrich d'Arrest found Neptune less than a degree from Le Verrier's spot. Some astronomers had wondered whether Newton's law failed so far from the Sun; instead the law had led to a new planet, showing that it held even at the edge of the known solar system.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks how a law is tested by its predictions, and Neptune, found where the law said it must be, is the standard example.

questions.question: Urbain Le Verrier, whose sums had led to Neptune, found in 1859 that the point of Mercury's orbit nearest the Sun creeps round a little faster than Newton's law and the pulls of the other planets allow. He blamed unseen matter closer to the Sun, as an unseen planet had explained the drift of Uranus. What accounted for Mercury's extra creep in the end?
questions.answer: Albert Einstein's new theory of gravity
choices: Albert Einstein's new theory of gravity
Asaph Hall's tiny change to the square in Newton's law
A belt of small rocks circling inside its path
Drag from the thin gas lying around the Sun
questions.context: No unseen planet or belt of rocks ever turned up, and Asaph Hall's idea of 1894, a pull falling with distance to the power 2.00000016 instead of 2, was a patch made to fit and was given up. In 1915 Einstein's general theory of relativity, which treats gravity as mass curving space and time, gave the missing 43 arcseconds a century with no patch at all. Newton's law is still an excellent guide for nearly every orbit; relativity is needed only where very strong gravity or extreme accuracy calls for it, and Mercury's tiny extra creep is such a case.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade courses name Einstein among the makers of modern physics, and Mercury's orbit is the honest case where a well-tested law needed a deeper theory.

questions.question: Henry Cavendish hung a rod nearly 2 metres long from a thin wire, with a small lead ball at each end, and set a lead ball of about 158 kilograms beside each small one. From how far their pull turned the rod, set beside Earth's own pull on the small balls, he found in 1798 that Earth is on average about 5.5 times as dense as water. What did that show about Earth?
questions.answer: Its inside is far denser than its surface rock
choices: Its inside is far denser than its surface rock
Its inside is about as dense as its surface rock
Its inside is less dense than its surface rock
Its inside is hollow, with shells within its crust
questions.context: The rocks of Earth's crust are only about 2.7 to 3 times as dense as water, so to bring the average up to 5.5, Earth's deep inside must be far denser: early evidence for a heavy metal core. Edmond Halley had suggested in 1692 that Earth is hollow, with shells nested inside, but no hollow Earth could weigh so much. With Earth's size, the density gave its mass, which is why the experiment is called weighing the Earth; Cavendish's figure, 5.45 once a slip in his sums was put right, sits close to today's 5.51.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches how indirect measurements reveal Earth's interior, and Cavendish's density, resting on the law of gravitation, is the first such clue.
